opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the big one I keep seeing is that people take an agent framework, point it at their internal APIs, and expect it to just work the way the demos do. And it usually doesn't, for a pretty fundamental reason: the frontier models have never seen your internal tools. They've seen tons of public APIs and open-source code during training, so they're reasonably good with things like GitHub or Stripe. But your company's billing service, or some internal data-access layer with its own quirks, its own naming conventions, its own weird error codes, is completely new to them.

So what happens is you get agents that look fine on a handful of happy-path examples, but once you put them on real workflows, they start calling the wrong tool, passing slightly malformed arguments, chaining calls in the wrong order, or misreading what a response actually means. And because these are multi-step tasks, small error rates compound. If each step is ninety percent reliable and the task takes eight or ten steps, your end-to-end success rate falls apart.

The usual response is prompt engineering: you stuff more documentation into the context, add more examples, write longer tool descriptions. That helps up to a point, but it gets brittle and expensive, and you hit a ceiling. What people really need is a way to specialize the model to their environment, to generate realistic tasks against their own tools, evaluate the agent properly, and then actually train it, whether that's fine-tuning or reinforcement learning, so it learns how *their* system behaves. That's the gap I think a lot of teams run into: there's no good pipeline for going from "here are my APIs" to "here's an agent that reliably works with them." And evaluation is a big part of that. Many teams don't really know how good or bad their agent is until it's already in front of users.

r001.rationale: The response says internal tools have their own quirks, naming conventions, and error codes, but frames the problem as models being unfamiliar with them. It does not clearly identify fragmentation of internal APIs and tools as the problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So the problem I keep running into, and the thing that actually got us started on Bespoke Labs, is that the agent demos look great and then they fall apart the moment you point them at a company's real internal tools.

When you build an agent on public APIs, the model has basically seen those APIs in pretraining. It knows what a Stripe call looks like, it knows GitHub, it knows the Google Calendar surface. So tool calling feels almost free. But inside a company you've got hundreds or thousands of internal endpoints, nobody's ever written good documentation for them, the parameter names are weird, there's implicit state, and there are business rules that live in someone's head rather than in the schema. The model has zero prior on any of that. So you get an agent that picks the wrong tool, fills in arguments that are syntactically valid but semantically wrong, or chains three calls together in an order that doesn't actually make sense for that system.

And the thing people try first is prompting. They dump the OpenAPI spec into the context, maybe write some few-shot examples, and it works for the five cases they tested. Then it hits the long tail and the accuracy drops to a point where you can't ship it. The frontier models are great general reasoners, but general reasoning doesn't tell you that in your billing system you have to call lookup-account before you can call apply-credit, or that this one field is actually a legacy ID and not the one the name suggests.

So the way I frame it is that this is really a data problem, not a model problem. You don't need a smarter model, you need the model to have actually experienced your environment. And the hard part is that nobody has the trajectories. There's no dataset of "here's a user request, here's the correct sequence of calls against our internal tools, here's what success looks like." Generating that data, generating it at scale and at high quality, and then using it to either fine-tune a smaller model or do RL in an environment that mirrors the real tools, that's where I think most of the leverage is right now. That's what we've been obsessed with.

r001.rationale: The response describes companies having hundreds or thousands of internal endpoints with undocumented interfaces, unusual parameter names, implicit state, and hidden business rules, making agents choose and use tools incorrectly.

astra-6.text:
One problem we see is that internal APIs weren’t designed with an AI agent in mind. They were designed for a developer who has context about how the system works. The developer knows which API to call, what the parameters mean, and which calls need to happen first. When you give those same APIs to an agent, that context is often missing.

So connecting the agent to the tools is only part of the work. You also need to make it clear when to use each tool, what it expects, and how to interpret the result. If you have several tools with overlapping functionality, even choosing the right one becomes difficult. The challenge is turning access to your APIs into something the agent can use reliably to accomplish a task.

r001.rationale: The response describes missing context and difficulty choosing among overlapping tools, but it does not clearly identify fragmentation of internal APIs and tools as the problem.

sol-6.1.text:
One problem is that internal APIs were usually designed for developers who already understand the system. There’s a lot of context that never makes it into the API description: which tool to use, what an argument actually means, or which calls have to happen first. When you give those same APIs to an agent, you’re asking it to infer all of that.

So an API can work perfectly well and still be difficult for an agent to use reliably. The challenge is making those tools understandable—giving the agent clear descriptions, useful examples, and errors that help it recover when something goes wrong.

r001.rationale: The response describes missing context in API descriptions and difficulty choosing tools or sequencing calls, but it does not clearly identify fragmentation of internal APIs and tools as the problem.
